content: The second review focused on the self-administration of medications for medical abortion and included 18 studies conducted in Albania, Bangladesh, China, France, India, Nigeria, Tunisia, Turkey, and Vietnam. A detailed summary of the evidence is available in Supplementary Material 2, which includes the Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) framework on self-management of medical abortion. The expert panel discussed the feasibility of this intervention in specific scenarios, such as when a woman has regular menstrual cycles, a known last menstrual period (LMP), and access to validated tools. Women, when provided with the necessary information, are capable of determining their eligibility for medical abortion. Considering the values, preferences, and high acceptability of this approach, the panel concluded that the intervention is favorable. Evidence indicates that self-administration of medications for medical abortion is effective (moderate certainty) and safe (low certainty). Women reported high satisfaction with self-administering their medications for abortion (very low-certainty evidence). Adherence to the medical abortion regimen was high (low-certainty evidence). The high acceptability and feasibility of this approach support its implementation. Regarding self-assessment of abortion success, high-certainty evidence shows that self-assessment using tools such as low-sensitivity pregnancy tests or multi-level pregnancy tests is as effective as assessments conducted by trained health workers. Low-certainty evidence suggests that women in the self-assessment group expressed greater satisfaction with the process. Implementation Considerations: Individuals must have access to accurate information about the self-management process and other available options within their local context to make informed decisions about whether to self-manage all or parts of the process. Self-assessment of eligibility includes determining pregnancy duration based on LMP. Tools, either paper-based or digital, can assist in recalling and calculating pregnancy duration or using checklists for eligibility assessment. Women with irregular menstrual cycles or other concerns should be encouraged to seek support from trained health workers when possible. Self-administration of medications involves taking some or all abortion medications without direct supervision from a health worker. It is crucial that all sources of medication provide quality-assured products. Women should be informed about potential pain during the process and have access to medications for pain management. Self-assessment of abortion success can be facilitated using checklists of signs and symptoms. Low-sensitivity urine pregnancy tests, which differ from standard pregnancy tests, may assist in confirming completion. High-sensitivity pregnancy tests, such as multi-level pregnancy tests (MLPT), used alone or with checklists, have shown higher sensitivity in detecting successful abortion outcomes. Access to health workers or healthcare facilities should be available to confirm abortion success or manage side effects or complications. Health workers and managers should recognize self-management as a legitimate pathway to abortion care and adapt health systems to support women in self-managing abortion, such as by modifying clinical protocols. Mechanisms should be established to ensure access or referrals to post-abortion contraception services and provide contraception for women who desire it. While self-management can improve health system efficiency in the long term, it should not shift the financial burden of healthcare services onto women. Post-Abortion Contraception: All contraceptive options may be considered after an abortion. Self-procured methods, such as over-the-counter or online options, including barrier methods, some hormonal contraceptives, oral contraceptive pills (OCPs), and emergency contraceptive pills, are generally available without a prescription. Shifting to self-management approaches, such as over-the-counter OCPs and self-injection of hormonal contraceptives, may improve contraceptive continuation by removing barriers like frequent visits to healthcare facilities. These approaches could expand access to contraception for individuals facing challenges in accessing healthcare settings regularly or in areas with health worker shortages, potentially reducing unintended pregnancies. WHO Recommendations: Self-administration of injectable contraception (initiation and continuation) is recommended in the post-abortion period. Injectable contraceptives can be administered intramuscularly or subcutaneously, and compact pre-filled auto-disable devices have been developed to facilitate self-administration. Evidence suggests higher continuation rates and satisfaction among self-administration users compared to clinic-based providers. This option may save time and financial resources for women while increasing autonomy and choice in contraceptive use within a rights-based framework. Over-the-counter oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) should be made available without a prescription for individuals using OCPs. Over-the-counter emergency contraceptive pills should also be made available without a prescription for individuals seeking emergency contraception. Consistent and correct use of male and female condoms is highly effective in preventing the sexual transmission of HIV, reducing the risk of acquiring other sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and preventing unintended pregnancies. Implementation Considerations for OCPs: Provide up to a one-year supply of pills based on the woman’s preference and anticipated use. Programs must balance the goal of maximizing access to pills with concerns about contraceptive supply and logistics. Key Human Rights Considerations: Sexual and reproductive health (SRH) care must be available, accessible, acceptable, and of good quality. States must ensure the availability of a wide range of modern, safe, and affordable contraceptive methods and adequate access to essential medicines in an affordable and non-discriminatory manner. States must respect autonomous decision-making, non-discrimination, and equality. This includes repealing or reforming laws and policies that impair individuals’ ability to realize their right to SRH, such as criminalizing abortion or imposing restrictive abortion laws. States must provide accurate, evidence-based abortion information confidentially and take steps to reduce maternal mortality and morbidity. Self-management of abortion should not be criminalized, as criminalization may create delays or barriers to seeking assistance or post-abortion care when needed. Self-management of medical abortion should be available based on clinical appropriateness and not restricted for non-clinical reasons such as age. Dissemination and Implementation of Guidelines: The guideline will be published digitally (interactive web-based version and downloadable document) and in print. Translations into Spanish, French, and Portuguese are planned, with other United Nations languages developed as needed. Derivative products, such as operational guidance, informational materials, pocket charts for health workers, decision-support tools, and case studies, will be developed to support implementation. WHO will collaborate with relevant United Nations agencies to disseminate guidance and tools to support a human rights-based approach to SRH and respond to country requests for technical assistance. Evaluation of Implementation and Impact: Implementation requires a multifaceted approach, including workshops and training programs to familiarize users with the guideline. WHO team members will engage with healthcare facility managers and staff to integrate the guidance into clinical support systems. Ongoing evaluation during the first year of implementation will focus on accessibility, acceptance, use, impact, and generalizability of the guideline and its recommendations. Monitoring will include engagement with the online version, document downloads, and distribution of hard copies.
